concrete_topics.title: Expression of alternative reproductive tactics relative to social context
concrete_topics.topic_description: Species with intense male-male competition for access to females often show alternative reproductive tactics (ARTs), with males of lower competitive ability trying to steal mates from courting rivals. In Drosophila prolongata, for example, non-courting males sometimes intercept the female from a courting male. This ART appears to be condition-dependent, but little is known about how the social context might influence its expression. We plan to test how varying local densities and sex ratios influence the expression of interception in D. prolongata in the context of frequency- and density-dependent selection. Evaluating the environmental and social factors promoting the expression of this ART is important to understand the maintenance of phenotypic variation on secondary sexual traits.

concrete_topics.title: Fitness consequences of heat stress across generations
concrete_topics.topic_description: Climate change is causing more extreme temperature fluctuations, including more widespread, longer, and more intense heatwaves. Extreme weather events can have damaging effects on organisms and cause species declines, extinctions, or range shifts across ecosystems. Animals like insects, whose physiology and metabolism are directly linked to their ambient temperature, are particularly affected. For better predictions of population distributions and persistence, we need to know how extreme conditions not only affect the survival of individuals but also their ability to reproduce. For example, there is growing evidence that heat stress can cause infertility in insects (e.g., due to sperm damage), but individuals below the sterility threshold may be affected in their own, but unexplored, way. Using experimental heatwaves at different life stages in our insect model systems (e.g., Drosophila), this project will explore (1) the short- and long-term fertility loss in exposed individuals, and (2) the health and fertility consequences for their offspring (i.e., transgenerational effects). A Master’s student will work alongside PhD student and conduct their independent research as part of a bigger project.

concrete_topics.title: Molecular mechanisms that allow bacteria to “innovate” antibiotic molecules
concrete_topics.topic_description: Project to uncover molecular, biochemical and evolutionary mechanisms that allow biosynthetic genes to diversify and produce novel natural-product antibiotics, with the long-term aim of harnessing those insights for bioengineering. The student will experimentally study a newly identified genetic element (GRINS), measuring its propagation frequency in model E. coli and comparing that to the high frequency seen in Streptomyces, using molecular cloning, gene editing and genetic assays (DNA extraction, PCR, cloning). The project is experimental, flexible in duration (3–9 months full- or part-time) and suited to motivated students willing to learn microbiology and molecular biology techniques.

concrete_topics.title: Behavioural projects on wild house mice at the barn
concrete_topics.topic_description: We run a long term field study (20+ years) on a large population of wild house mice outside of Zurich, enabling a variety of projects in animal behaviour. House mice are wonderful study organisms as we can directly observe them and collect data on many aspects of their behaviour, for a large number of animals. We can obtain fitness measurements over several generations in a fairly short period of time to test the fitness consequences of alternative behaviours. We provide living conditions that mice like, and many stay, despite the possibility to emigrate. The wild house mice can also be brought to the lab for controlled experiments. We offer a variety of projects investigating social behaviour. House mice are social animals, and studying social interactions provides insights into how and why animals form societies. Some examples of projects that could be the basis of a MSc project are the following: 1) The role of vocalisations in house mice social relationships. Mice vocalise regularly, and their vocalisations have been compared to birdsong in its complexity, but what is the function of these vocalisations? Experimental playbacks can be used to test how mice interpret the vocalisations of other individuals. 2) Mice live together in a home range, either in the same home range they were born into, or another, but interact unequally with other individuals. In the main breeding season, females also reduce the number of other mice that they live with, and many breed plurally, pooling litters and sharing the care of offspring. How do mice choose their social partners? An analysis of our huge dataset allows tests of which features are most important. 3) Mice have complex social relationships, and cooperate and compete with each other. To what extent do mice have individually differentiated social relationships with their nestmates? Using cameras house mice can be observed without disturbing them, allowing analyses that have never been done before. 4) Mice can live a long time. Do social interactions change with age? 5) In the lab, males provide some parental care. In the wild, we think that they do not, because they have other reproductive prospects to pursue. Are wild male mice caring for offspring? We can use cameras to observe pups in the nest, and determine if and to what extent males are caring for pups. We also combine social behaviour with fitness data. We find that some females (about 50%!) are reproductively suppressed, producing no offspring, while others produce up more than ten litters. What determines who fails at the most important task of all, reproduction? Do dominance interactions predict reproduction in females, as is thought to be the case in males? We have a large dataset available, and cameras at nests can be used to compare interactions between individuals, and how individuals invest into maternal care. How do females choose males? How does male quality differ, and does it matter for her fitness? We study dispersal, and aim to understand how and why mice disperse both within and outside the population. Leaving the population is risky, because, for a commensal species, suitable habitats are patchy, and predators are abundant. Not leaving is also risky, because many mice fail to reproduce. Who leaves, and why? What about immigration? We also have predation events, and do not yet understand what makes some mice more susceptible to predation. What makes a mouse a survivor? We study domestication, aiming to understand how mice have adapted to our research project over 20 years! We have documented an increase in white pigmentation, and a decrease in head length over time, consistent with predictions of the domestication syndrome. We aim to continue this study of signs of domestication. We study inbreeding, and are interested in determining which mice inbreed and how strong the fitness consequences are. We are also interested in recent findings that house mice perform “first aid” on each other DOI: 10.1126/science.adv3731, and that chance early life effects have a large influence on fitness outcomes DOI: 10.1126/science.adq0579. We are open to other topics as well. Requirements Curiousity about animal behaviour Willingness to obtain training to work with live house mice Willingness to participate in field or lab work Ability for teamwork Project start Anytime – open to discussion (anna.lindholm@ieu.uzh.ch) Department of Evolutionary Biology and Environmental Studies, University of Zurich

concrete_topics.title: Behavioural projects relevant to ethical mouse biocontrol
concrete_topics.topic_description: We are developing a project on biocontrol of house mice. House mice are generalists which have been introduced to many parts of the world, including regions where their natural enemies are absent. As they are flexible in their behaviour and reproduce quickly when conditions are favourable, mouse populations easily build up. This can become a problem, for example, when crops and food stores are spoiled, or mice learn to prey upon endemic invertebrate or bird species. The current method of mouse control relies on applications of poison. Our project relies on the t-haplotype, a large natural genetic polymorphism which acts as a male meiotic driver, and which, when homozygous, destroys its carrier’s sperm production, thereby interfering with reproduction. Thus in males, only heterozygotes transmit the t haplotype to offspring (but at a high rate: 80-95% of offspring!). We are testing the extent to which the t-haplotype influences social behaviour and female mate choice and its rate of spread in populations, and offer several MSc projects. Social interactions House mice carrying the t-haplotype are more likely to leave a population than wild-type individuals, but the underlying processes and the differences between genotypes are poorly understood. How do social interactions of t carriers and wildtype mice influence access to resources, such as food, nest sites, and females, as well as the decision to disperse? Automated motion tracking will be used to analyse social behaviour of individual mice. i) In this project, the student will contribute to a large experiment investigating the processes that lead to dispersal in house mice. The student will train annotations using DeepLabCut to track social behaviour in the video data from these experiments. The data will then be analysed to assess the social relationships between individuals. Furthermore, the results can be linked to the already analysed anxiety and exploratory behaviour of these individuals. This study will contribute to our understanding of how the t-haplotype spreads in nature. Mice are a mammalian model species, and understanding dispersal in house mice will also help to understand how and why animals disperse in general, a particularly important topic in projecting changes in animal distributions over time. ii) Male house mice carrying the t-haplotype appear to influence the reproductive success of their neighbours negatively. We aim to understand how, testing hypotheses about social hierarchy, and positive and negative social interactions in experimental settings. The student will train annotations using DeepLabCut to track social behaviour in the video data from these experiments. The data will then be analysed to assess the social relationships between individuals, and the results related to which individuals gain or lose fitness. This is a key aspect to understanding how t-carriers influence population reproductive success. Mate choice experiments Our project relies on transmission of the t-haplotype between generations, and therefore on female interest in mating with t-haplotype carrying males. We are experimentally testing various aspects of female mate preferences, such as the extent to which phenotypic differences between males (such as body size differences) influence female mate preferences, as this could be used to improve the mating prospects of t-haplotype carriers, for example, by giving them access to growth-maximising conditions. What influences frequencies of a meiotic driver in nature? One of the best known male meiotic drivers is the t-haplotype, which occurs in wild populations of house mice in Switzerland and elsewhere. The t-haplotype is a supergene that influences sperm competition – in heterozygotes giving an advantage to t over + sperm in within-male sperm competition for fertilisation, resulting in super-Mendelian inheritance patterns. However, it has a large disadvantage in between-male sperm competition, and harmful recessive effects, which brake its spread in nature. It is found in mouse populations all over the world, but no one has yet undertaken a global analysis of t-frequencies and distribution. The student will develop hypotheses and test them using data from the literature and our own data. We also offer possibilities for more theoretical approaches to predicting t-frequencies in nature, and studying t-haplotype evolution. Requirements Curiousity about animal behaviour Willingness to participate in ongoing field or lab work Aptitude for teamwork Project start Anytime – open to discussion (anna.lindholm@ieu.uzh.ch) Department of Evolutionary Biology and Environmental Studies, University of Zurich

concrete_topics.title: Innovation and culture in urban-living cockatoos
concrete_topics.topic_description: The capacity for innovation, social learning and culture is vital to the success of humans, facilitating our colonization of almost every habitat on Earth. But has culture been a determinant of success in any other species? Urban environments present a natural experiment to investigate these questions, as cities provide novel challenges and opportunities that animals need to respond to over short time-scales. Our recent research on one urban-adaptor, the sulphur-crested cockatoo, has described the spread of one innovation, flipping bin lids to raid household food scraps in Sydney Australia. In this work, and the help of citizen-science, we mapped emergence and geographic spread of this behaviour to observe the formation of a local ‘bin-opening culture’. However, people have now responded to this behaviour by protecting bins with a variety of methods. Our evidence for social learning of bin protection by people (and anecdotal observations that birds can defeat measures) leads to the potential for an interspecies cultural arms race. This masters project will investigate whether this is occurring by using a combination of observations and experiments to test where, when and how cockatoos can defeat bin protection measures. The project will combine spatial mapping and citizen science approaches with wild fieldwork on habituated cockatoos in eastern Australia. Requirements An interest in animal behaviour and cognition. Experience with programming or statistics in R or Python, or a strong motivation to learn. A willingness to engage with a large, active, and exciting research team. Willingness to engage in urban/peri-urban fieldwork in Australia, and a current passport. Project start Starting date open If you want to know more about our lab and projects visit our website . If you are interested in this work, please send an email with a brief letter of motivation (1-2 paragraphs) outlining why you wish to join the project to: , Department of Evolutionary Biology and Environmental Studies, University of Zurich, Switzerland

concrete_topics.title: Experimental study of meerkats’ orientation and navigation mechanisms
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project experimentally tests whether meerkats use the sun as a compass and what environmental features (landmarks, specific routes) they use to navigate their territory. The student will do fieldwork (2–4 months) at the Kalahari Research Centre deploying GPS tracking experiments on wild meerkats and then apply spatial-ecology analyses and modelling (using R) on the collected data, based at the University of Zurich.

concrete_topics.title: Sexual conflict in chacma baboons
concrete_topics.topic_description: Project description I am advertising MSc projects focusing on wild chacma baboons in the Waterberg district of the Limpopo province, South Africa. The main research goal is to improve our understanding of the role of sexual conflict as a selection pressure shaping physiology, male-female relationships, and paternal behavior. Together with local and international field assistants and students, you will collect behavioral, endocrinological, genetic and ecological data while following habituated chacma baboon troops. The study site – also home to vervet monkeys and bushbabies, to name only the primates – is located on the Swebeswebe Wildlife Estate, approximately 50km from the town of Lephalale. You will also contribute to the general running of the research camp set in the rugged bushveld with magnificent wildlife. The research camp provides all necessary amenities including free fast internet access. Requirements You should be in possession or close to obtaining a bachelor’s degree in biology or Biomedicine from the University of Zurich (or another Swiss University). Previous field experience is desirable, but not essential. You should be physically fit and resilient. Project start Start dates of MSc Projects are flexible. Also visit the website Primate Reproductive Strategies and Socioendocrinology

concrete_topics.title: The use of Alarm Call vocalizations in a Semi-Urban population of vervet monkeys
concrete_topics.topic_description: This MSc project will focus on identifying the acoustic variation in alarm calls related to the context in which they are produced in a semi urban vervet monkey population. In particular, we are interested in studying responses to dogs, and other anthropogenic introduced threats in the habitat of this population. The project entails 6-8 months field work at the Simbithi Eco Estate at the East Coast of South Africa. You will be working in a small team and beside recording monkey vocalizations you will contribute to the projects general data collection. Requirements An interest in animal behaviour and animal communication. Preferrable but not required computer programming experience (e.g. in R). Willingness to spend prolonged time in South Africa with physically hard work following vervet monkeys in a semi-urban habitat. Great interest in cross-cultural teamwork. Project start Enrolment as MSc student at Animal Behaviour Group from Fall Semester 2023. Fieldwork period January 2024 (7-8 months). Applications should include a CV and a motivation letter why you are particularly suited/ interested in this research. If you are interested or would like to have further information regarding this project, please don’t hesitate to reach out to us: Department of Evolutionary Biology and Environmental Studies, University of Zurich, Switzerland , Department of Evolutionary Biology and Environmental Studies, University of Zurich, Switzerland More information about our research groups under: Animal Curiosity and Cognition Communication and Cognition in Social Mammals

concrete_topics.title: Vocal activity and flexibility in call usage in wild meerkats
concrete_topics.topic_description: This project investigates how behavioural and social contexts affect meerkat calling rate and whether meerkats show vocal flexibility by using similar call types across multiple contexts. The student will do 2–4 months of fieldwork at the Kalahari Research Centre and work at the University of Zurich collecting audio and video, annotating recordings, performing acoustic analyses, processing data and running statistics in R, and producing a scientific thesis.

concrete_topics.title: Vocal communication in yellow mangooses
concrete_topics.topic_description: This Master’s thesis aims to investigate vocal communication in yellow mongooses to contribute to understanding the communication system of this rarely studied species. The student will conduct fieldwork at the Kalahari Research Centre in northwest South Africa (planned field season starting February 2025, 3–6 months, with a potential Master’s start in September 2024) studying vocal behaviour and social organization in small family groups of this facultatively social, small carnivore.

process.process_description: Master’s candidates choose an available topic or propose a self‑selected topic to a supervisor (internal or external). In addition to the supervisor, a faculty member or other person with “Promotionsrecht” must agree to supervise. Topics are listed on unit webpages and in the department’s research‑group/topic lists; past and ongoing theses are published there. To start, upload the Master’s agreement and a 2–3 (30 ECTS) / 4–6 (60 ECTS) page draft concept on Lean Gate; once accepted by supervisor and the Promotionsrecht person it is assigned automatically. Book the corresponding module (GEO/ESS 511 for 30 ECTS or GEO/ESS 510 for 60 ECTS) in UZH’s module booking tool — from autumn 2024 starts are allowed monthly (start = 1st of month); January starters must email teaching-support@geo.uzh.ch for manual booking. Duration: 30 ECTS = 6–12 months, 60 ECTS = 12–18 months. Official timelines, topic lists and guidelines (including plagiarism rules) are on the department pages, the timetable link and UZH’s plagiarism webpage.

process.process_description: The Bachelor thesis (12 ECTS) is written in the 6th semester, offered only in the spring, and is an individual literature-based paper. Admission requires successful completion of compulsory modules from semesters 1–3; it is recommended to choose a topic in an area where you took an elective. An information event takes place in October. Topics are published (typically Nov), supervisors and topics are announced (ESS 388: topic and supervisor on 24.10 in the example schedule) and students register (e.g. notify Meredith C. Schuman for ESS 388 and book the ESS 388 module), enroll in GEO 386 or ESS 386 and in lean-gate.geo.uzh.ch. A supervisor-confirmed concept must be submitted (deadline example 12.12), and final digital submission is via Lean Gate (GEO386/ESS386) or OLAT (ESS388) (example deadline 15.05). Deregistration deadline, presentation and grading dates, resit policy (one repeat allowed), plagiarism rules, evaluation criteria and full formal requirements are given in the linked information sheet, evaluation table and FAQs on the department webpage.

concrete_topics.title: Diverse topics in palaeo-ecology and macroevolution
concrete_topics.topic_description: Within evolutionary research, palaeontology uniquely allows for the study of (1) evolution in its ecological context (palaeo-ecology) and (2) the long-term fate of species and higher-rank taxa through geologic time (macroevolution). I am flexible in offering topics for master theses in both areas. Typically, palaeo-ecological studies will be based on own fieldwork, whereas studies in macroevolution make use of literature data and museum collections. Do not hesitate to contact me if you are interested in contributing to our understanding on how life on Earth evolved from a palaeontological perspective!

concrete_topics.title: Diverse topics in Palynology/Palaeobotany
concrete_topics.topic_description: Palynology is the study of microscopic resistant-walled fossils of various plants, animals and protists. It offers a wide range of interesting master's theses. The analysis of spore and pollen associations through time allows for reconstruction of past vegetation composition and terrestrial ecosystem dynamics but also to detect evolutionary pathways in plants. Spore-pollen analyses are also used as valuable climate proxy. Palynofacies analysis includes not only palynomorphs, such as spores and pollen grains, but also palynodebris such as wood particles, cuticles, algae, etc. thus describing the entire assemblages of particulate organic matter. Thus, palynofacies describes the depositional environment of the studied sample and is often used for basin analysis (e.g. sea-level changes, petroleum exploration). Please do not hesitate to contact Dr. Elke Schneebeli for further information.

concrete_topics.title: Diversifizierung und Aussterben von Mysidioptera und Plagiostoma
concrete_topics.topic_description: Mysidioptera ist eine Gattung der Feilenmuscheln (Limidae), die in der Mittel- und frühen Obertrias innerhalb relativ kurzer Zeit extrem schnell diversifizierte (über 100 beschriebene Arten), aber gegen Ende der Trias wieder ausstarb. Dieses Muster steht im Gegensatz zur etwa zeitgleich entstandenen Gattung Plagiostoma aus der gleichen Familie, die niemals eine so grosse Diversität wie Mysidioptera erreichte, dafür aber wesentlich langlebiger war und erst in die Kreide ausstarb. Die beiden nah verwandten und ökologisch vergleichbaren Gattungen stehen damit stellvertretend für zwei sehr unterschiedliche Diversitäts-Dynamiken: "boom and bust" Dynamik ( Mysidioptera ) versus Gleichgewichtsdynamik ( Plagiostoma ). In der Masterarbeit sollen die Diversitäts-Dynamiken der beiden Gattungen in der Trias auf Grundlage von Literaturstudium und Sammlungsmaterial rekonstruiert werden und Gründe für die unterschiedlichen Speziations- und Aussterbe-Dynamik erschlossen werden. Aus dieser Fallstudie werden allgemeine Erkenntnisse über die Steuerungsfaktoren von unterschiedlichen Diversitäts-Dynamiken erwartet, die sich auf andere Gruppen übertragen lassen.

concrete_topics.title: Evolutionary trends in the ornamentation of bivalves
concrete_topics.topic_description: The ornamentation of bivalves, which includes all external morphological features of the shell such as ribs, knots or spines, is often an adaptation to particular functions. It may support burrowing in soft or hard substratum, strengthen the rigidity of the shell in the face of high water energy, enable weight reduction, or help defending the animal against predators. Trends in the relative frequencies of different types of ornamentation over geologic times are therefore expected to reflect changes in the ecological regime (such as the evolution of competitors and predators), changes of the physical environment, or evolutionary innovations related to the occupation of new niches. The project aims at analyzing evolutionary trends in the ornamentation of bivalve shells in this context. It will consist of three main steps: (1) defining different categories of shell ornamentation; (2) documenting relative frequencies of these categories in bivalve genera from the Cambrian to the Recent, based on the Treatise on Invertebrate Paleontology and primary literature, and (3) analyzing the dataset with respect to potential driving forces. As such, the project results will add to our understanding of macroecological trends in a major class of marine invertebrates.

concrete_topics.title: Morphological diversification of Betta fish and of cichlids in the domestication process
concrete_topics.topic_description: Using state-of-the-art non-invasive imaging and morphospace quantification methods, the goal is the characterize the morphological diversification of some fish domestic species in the evolutionary context of their group. Morphologcail novelties have arisen due to artificial selection for ornamental traits, and we will explore how these relate to the evolvability of such traits in macroevolution. It is a project appropriate to those interested in working with 3D imaging, morphometrics and analyses of morphological evolution.

concrete_topics.title: Numerous topics in paleobiology and evolutionary morphology of terrestrial vertebrates
concrete_topics.topic_description: In the research group "Evolutionary Morphology and Paleobiology" (Prof. Sánchez, Prof. Dr. Scheyer and colleagues) we offer different master thesis topics. We mainly deal with different aspects of vertebrate evolution and developmental biology. Our facilities include a wet lab for tissue science, morphometrics studies and similar ontogenetic studies, and a paleohistology lab where we study the structure and evolution of fossil hard tissues. On the Lab website www.msanchezlab.net you can find a list of our current research topics and information about topics for master theses in our group. There you can also learn more about all members of the group, their research interests and publications. Please contact Prof. Sánchez or Prof. Dr. Scheyer for further details.

concrete_topics.title: Paläo-Ökologie benthischer Faunengemeinschaften aus dem Unterjura Mitteleuropas
concrete_topics.topic_description: Am Übergang von der Trias in den Jura fand eines der fünf grössten Massenaussterbe-Ereignisse der Erdgeschichte statt. Im Gegensatz zu anderen Massenaussterbe-Ereignissen konnte sich jedoch die benthische Lebewelt sehr schnell wieder erholen. Die post-extinction -Faunen des Unterjura sind daher deutlich diverser und ökologisch heterogener als solche nach anderen Aussterbe-Ereignissen. In dem Projekt soll erstmals eine moderne ökologische Analyse benthischer Faunengemeinschaften aus dem basalen Unterjura Mitteleuropas durchgeführt werden. Dazu sind Neuaufsammlungen geplant, die mit der Auswertung von Sammlungsmaterial kombiniert werden sollen. Im Ergebnis sollen die post-extinction Faunen des Unterjura paläo-ökologisch charakterisiert und mit ähnlichen Faunengemeinschaften aus der Zeit nach dem endpermischen Massenaussterben verglichen werden. Unterschiede zwischen diesen Faunengemeinschaften sollen herausgearbeitet werden mit dem Ziel, ein generelles konzeptionelles Verständnis für die ökologischen Prozesse zu entwickeln, die im Anschluss an globale Umweltkatastrophen wirksam sind.

concrete_topics.title: Paleoecology of neotropical aquatic communities
concrete_topics.topic_description: The Neogene sedimentary sequence in the Urumaco region, Western Venezuela (South Caribbean), is well known by its diverse continental and aquatic fauna from the middle Miocene-early Pliocene, providing unequivocal evidence of a large river system that flowed from far south in western Amazonia into the Caribbean. This project contemplates the study of marine and continental vertebrate remains, from ancient marine environments associated with freshwater inputs. This is a project suitable for those interested in paleodiversity, taxonomy and paleoecology, as well as fieldwork in the neotropics. Contact person

concrete_topics.title: Virtual invertebrate palaeontology applied to Devonian fossils
concrete_topics.topic_description: Methods of virtual palaeontology become increasingly important and more widely applied. For this Master-thesis, it is planned that the candidate will segment existing micro-CT image-stacks of Devonian invertebrates (arthropods, molluscs or else) in order to obtain good images of the fossils. These images will then be used to determine and describe the material and in some cases, new species can be described based on these materials. If time permits, constructional morphology as well as aspects of the animal's phylogeny can be studied as well.

concrete_topics.title: The fossil record of piranhas, tetras and other characiform fishes in the neotropics
concrete_topics.topic_description: New fossil discoveries from Cenozoic sites in South America document the deep evolutionary history of a diverse group of characiform fishes. Research consist of the screening of microvertebrate concentrations, familiarization with anatomy of fossil remains and systematic investigation of the phylogeny of the species involved. The fossils will serve to address questions of past biogeography and the antiquity of clades of fishes in the Proto-Amazonia River Basin. Contact person

process.process_description: Eligible students: enrolled Master’s students in Physics. Find a supervisor via the posted list of thesis topics or by contacting research groups directly; external internships are possible but require a UZH physics lecturer to accept formal responsibility and approve coursework. Register: record a Learning Agreement on studentadmin.mnf.uz.ch at the start of the Master’s and finalize it with your supervisor before starting the thesis. Sign up for the Masterprüfung by submitting the “Anmeldung Masterprüfung” form (signed by the supervisor) to studium@physik.uzh.ch at least 2 weeks before the desired Thursday seminar slot (Seminar für Bachelor- und Mastervorträge, Thu 15–17). Deadlines: the thesis must be handed to the supervisor at least 2 weeks before the exam. Requirements: 30 or 50 ECTS (≈6 or 10 months), public seminar + private oral exam (~30 min each), final grade = 2/3 written report + 1/3 oral; both components must be ≥4.0. Declare any AI tools used in References or the independence statement. Templates, forms and official guidelines are on the department pages (studentadmin.mnf.uz.ch and the department’s forms page).

Die Bachelorarbeit wird in der Regel im letzten Bachelorsemester durchgeführt und ist Voraussetzung für ein Masterstudium. concrete_topics.topic_description: Reimplement and benchmark the current commercial high-content microscopy image analysis pipeline for single-cell DNA damage and repair studies using the open-source Fractal platform, then develop and integrate AI-based methods available in Fractal to create a next-generation image analysis workflow. The student will recreate the existing pipeline, compare its performance to the commercial solution, and then upgrade it with cutting-edge machine-learning approaches using existing imaging datasets (with the option to acquire new images later).

concrete_topics.title: Label-Free Optical Microscopy and Machine Learning for Brain Cancer Research
concrete_topics.topic_description: Develop an experimental pipeline for label-free motility characterization of medulloblastoma cell models by building a label-free optical microscopy platform and advanced image analysis tools to reconstruct and quantify cell migration dynamics. The student will establish reproducible sample preparation for model and patient-derived cells, adapt and extend existing computational tools for cell tracking in label-free images, and perform extensive imaging and data analysis to characterize medulloblastoma responses to chemical perturbations.

concrete_topics.title: hematologic malignancies of childhood
concrete_topics.topic_description: You will investigate molecular mechanisms driving drug resistance and therapy failure in childhood leukemia using a bank of patient-derived xenograft samples to define dependencies and test therapeutic strategies. Depending on the chosen project you will perform experiments such as CRISPR genome editing and endogenous tagging of fusion oncogenes combined with affinity purification–mass spectrometry, RNA targeting of splicing variants, integrative genomic/transcriptomic analyses, high-content image-based drug screening, lentiviral transduction and selection of resistant populations, CAR T cell production/characterization and multiparametric flow cytometry to identify interactomes, resistance biomarkers and escape mechanisms. Projects range from mapping fusion transcription factor networks and aberrant splicing, to profiling longitudinal refractory samples, dissecting CAR T–mediated resistance, or characterizing AML vulnerabilities with emphasis on nuclear export and epigenetic modulation; supervision is provided by a postdoc or PhD student with regular PI meetings in an international lab.

concrete_topics.title: Mechanistic insights into Oncogene-Induced Replication Stress
concrete_topics.topic_description: Determine whether oncogenes such as MYC, BCR/ABL and BRAF induce R-loop–mediated replication stress in a ROS- and PRDX2-dependent manner, extending prior findings with oncogenic HRAS. The student will perform cell culture and lentiviral manipulations, DNA fiber spreading, immunofluorescence, chromatin immunoprecipitation, qRT-PCR, Cut&Tag and next‑generation sequencing, and carry out the accompanying bioinformatic analyses to assess replication dynamics, R-loops and PRDX2/ROS involvement. You will join the Janscak group investigating molecular mechanisms that maintain genome stability.

concrete_topics.title: Translational skin cancer research
concrete_topics.topic_description: The Levesque laboratory offers translational Master’s projects to dissect immune and metastatic mechanisms in skin cancers and uveal melanoma, including studying cuproptosis effects on tumor immune markers, melanoma–TLS crosstalk, mRNA immunocytokine/CAR T strategies, liver tropism in uveal melanoma, and resistance states in cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma. Students will perform experimental and computational work such as 2D/3D cell culture, flow cytometry, western blotting, proteomics, transcriptomics, CRISPR‑a/i screens, single‑cell and spatial transcriptomics, multiplex IHC/IF, ELISAs, and high‑throughput tumor killing assays to define pathways and validate targets. They will analyze multi‑omics and spatial data to map tumor ecosystems, model cell–cell communication and metastatic trajectories, and validate key interactions in patient‑derived cell lines and tissues. Projects leverage a large live‑cell skin‑cancer biobank and clinical collaborations to develop biomarkers, therapeutic targets and mechanistic models with translational potential.

concrete_topics.title: Advancing CAR T cell immunotherapy
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project aims to advance CAR T cell immunotherapy by engineering non-viral, Sleeping Beauty transposon–based CAR T cells to increase potency, prevent antigen-negative relapse, and overcome tumor microenvironment–induced T cell exhaustion. The student will design and test novel multi-targeting CAR combinations and combinatorial therapies, produce and functionally characterize engineered T cells in vitro, and perform proof-of-concept preclinical efficacy and safety studies in immunodeficient and humanized mouse cancer models. Techniques used include T cell culture and CAR production with Sleeping Beauty, CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, flow cytometry, molecular assays and microscopy.

concrete_topics.title: Pediatric Cancer Metabolism
concrete_topics.topic_description: Join the Morscher Lab to investigate pediatric cancer metabolism with the goal of identifying metabolic vulnerabilities and genetic determinants that enable non-genotoxic therapeutic strategies. In Project 1 you will run high-throughput screens on cell lines and patient-derived xenografts, test amino acid depletion sensitivities in vivo, quantify amino acids by LC–MS, perform immunofluorescent imaging, and use translation inhibitors and shRNA to evaluate and optimize nutritional and pharmacological combinations. In Project 2 you will use dCas9 osteosarcoma cell lines to perform a genome-wide CRISPRa/i screen under therapeutic pressure, validate candidate resistance genes and dissect their mechanisms using CRISPR/Cas9, automated drug screening, cell culture and multi-omics approaches.

concrete_topics.title: Genetically engineered organoids as in vitro and in vivo model systems of gastric cancer
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project develops genetically engineered murine gastric organoids as in vitro and in vivo models of gastric carcinogenesis by overexpressing oncogenes or deleting tumor suppressors using CRISPR and RNAi, then orthotopically transplanting the cells into the gastric submucosa of syngeneic immunocompetent mice. The student will perform genetic modification, orthotopic transplantations and downstream analyses including spectral flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, targeted and genome-wide CRISPR screens, drug testing, and functional studies of candidate tumor suppressors. Resulting tumor material will be analyzed by exome sequencing, bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry protocols and multiplex immunofluorescence microscopy, and projects may include studying effects of Helicobacter pylori infection and interactions with homologous recombination gene mutations on tumorigenesis and metastasis.

concrete_topics.title: Enhancing CAR T cell therapy for diffuse midline glioma through rational drug combinations
concrete_topics.topic_description: Project goal: identify rational small-molecule and CAR T cell combinations to enhance antitumor potency, overcome resistance, and improve clinical translatability of CAR T therapy for diffuse midline glioma (DMG). The student will perform hands-on work with primary human T cells and patient-derived DMG models including lentiviral CAR transduction, expansion and functional cytotoxicity assays, co-cultures, systematic drug-combination testing with dose–response and synergy analyses, and assays such as flow cytometry, cytokine profiling, live‑cell imaging, viability testing and optional CRISPR-Cas9 genome engineering. They will quantify CAR T activation, exhaustion, cytokine release and tumor-cell killing under combination treatments and participate in group meetings, journal clubs and progress reporting with daily supervision and the possibility to extend the project toward publication.

concrete_topics.title: Formal validation of CRISPR screen-identified hits in diffuse midline glioma
concrete_topics.topic_description: Validate CRISPR screen–identified candidate drivers of radio- and chemoresistance in diffuse midline glioma (DMG) and map the underlying resistance pathways to identify potential therapeutic targets. The student will generate and manipulate cell models (lentiviral production/transduction, CRISPR‑Cas9 editing, irradiation), run molecular and cellular assays (DNA/RNA extraction, Western blot, immunofluorescence, viability assays) and perform functional and omics-based analyses to characterize treatment-induced responses in vitro. Training and supervision are provided within the DMG/DIPG research group in collaboration with the Neuropathology Institute at Universitätsspital Zürich.

concrete_topics.title: The interferon system in the control of DNA replication and genome stability
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project aims to decipher the role of the Interferon/ISG15 system in maintenance of genome integrity, with a focus on its functions in the DNA damage response and DNA replication. The student will perform experiments using biochemistry, molecular and cellular biology, proteomics, CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing and screens, FACS, clonogenic assays, single DNA-molecule replication assays, immunofluorescence and quantitative imaging to analyze DNA replication and genome-stability phenotypes. The work will be carried out in the Penengo Lab at the Institute of Molecular Cancer Research (IMCR), with participation in lab meetings and journal clubs within an international research environment.

concrete_topics.title: Ubiquitin phosphorylation as new signaling system in genome stability
concrete_topics.topic_description: This Master thesis will investigate the dynamics of phosphorylated ubiquitin (phosphoUb) on chromatin to identify the kinases, ubiquitin ligases and other factors that constitute this novel phosphoUb-based signaling system controlling DNA double-strand break repair and genome stability. The student will use biochemical, molecular and cellular approaches — including proteomics, CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, FACS, clonogenic assays, single‑molecule DNA replication assays, immunofluorescence and quantitative imaging — to map pUb dynamics, identify interacting proteins and assess their functional roles in DNA repair.

concrete_topics.title: nucleolus and 3D genome in acute myeloid leukemia (AML)
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project aims to define how loss of NPM1 nucleolar functions contributes to malignant transformation in NPM1-mutant acute myeloid leukemia. The student will apply the NoLMseq single-cell nucleolar laser microdissection sequencing method to map changes in nucleolus–NAD interactions caused by NPM1c mislocalization, and perform transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses to characterize gene expression and chromatin features at affected NADs. Using well-established cellular models, they will dissect mechanisms by which NPM1c dysregulates nucleolar-associated chromatin and identify potential therapeutic vulnerabilities.

concrete_topics.title: Biochemical and Biophysical Characterization of Small-Molecule Inhibitors Targeting DNA Repair
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project aims to biochemically and biophysically characterize small-molecule inhibitors of the DNA repair nuclease FAN1, determining their binding affinity, selectivity and cellular efficacy to evaluate their potential as research tools or therapeutic leads. The MSc student will take hit compounds from ongoing high-throughput screens and apply biochemical, biophysical and cellular assays together with in silico computational tools to measure inhibition, guide optimization of lead chemistry, and integrate results with protein- and nuclease-based fluorescence assays. Practical work will involve molecular biology and protein biochemistry techniques, setting up and running the established HTS-derived assays, and analyzing data to prioritize and improve candidate inhibitors.

concrete_topics.title: Dissecting the regulators of oncoembryonic programs in colorectal cancer
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project aims to identify and functionally characterize regulators of oncoembryonic transcriptional programs in in vitro models of colorectal cancer. The student will use advanced CRC models (human and mouse organoids) to perturb candidate transcription factors, signaling pathways or chromatin regulators (CRISPR/Cas-based and/or chemical modulation), assess resulting cell-state changes by bulk and optional single-cell transcriptomics, and link these programs to proliferation, differentiation, stress tolerance or drug response. Training includes mammalian cell and organoid culture, molecular biology (cloning, qPCR, protein analysis), functional perturbation, RNA-seq analysis and microscopy, with possible exposure to epigenomic or advanced computational approaches.

concrete_topics.title: In vivo engineering of chimeric antigen receptor-based cell therapies for cancer therapy
concrete_topics.topic_description: The project aims to develop in vivo genetic reprogramming of immune cells to generate CAR-based cell therapies that can recognize, resist, and remodel the immunosuppressive microenvironment of solid tumors by delivering nucleic acids with immune-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Students would work on aspects such as LNP formulation and immune-cell–specific delivery, novel CAR designs (e.g., logic-gated or multi-antigen CARs), armoring strategies (siRNA/ASO checkpoint knockdown), mRNA engineering (sequence optimization, regulatory elements, circular RNA) and CRISPR/Cas approaches including large-fragment knock-ins for stable CAR expression. Projects commonly include in vivo evaluation of engineered CAR immune cells in solid tumor models and are offered as Master’s thesis or semester projects.

concrete_topics.title: MSc Position Cancer Biology
concrete_topics.topic_description: Study how newly identified microproteins discovered by translatome analyses regulate cellular homeostasis and cancer. You will pick a newly identified human or mouse microprotein and develop and execute a project to determine its role in cancer. The work involves large-scale data analysis, molecular cloning, cell culture and lentiviral methods, CRISPR, microscopy, FACS, protein and RNA assays, polysome/ribosome profiling and basic bioinformatics, with training in presentation and writing skills.

concrete_topics.title: Characterization of the effect of Notch signaling on cellular subpopulations in Rhabdomyosarcoma
concrete_topics.topic_description: This project aims to characterize how Notch signaling controls distinct cellular subpopulations in rhabdomyosarcoma and how its modulation affects therapy response. The student will optimize ex vivo culture conditions to better mimic the muscle stem cell niche and enhance Notch activation, perform targeted Notch disruption using CRISPR knockouts and pathway inhibitors to identify key regulators, and evaluate effects on cell proliferation and chemosensitivity. Finally, multiplex imaging will be used to spatially and quantitatively profile tumor subpopulations after Notch modulation alone or in combination with standard chemotherapy.

concrete_topics.title: Advancing therapeu1c strategies in liver metastasis
concrete_topics.topic_description: This MSc project aims to elucidate the immune landscape of colorectal liver metastasis (CRLM), focusing on how T cell–myeloid cell interactions and their spatial dynamics shape clinical outcomes and could inform new therapies. The student will experimentally and computationally characterize these interactions in CRLM using high-dimensional flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing and related computational workflows. The 9–12 month project is embedded in the Tugues Lab team with dedicated supervision and access to cutting-edge technologies.

process.process_description: This page concerns the Masterarbeit for Human‑ and Zahnmedizin Master students: the thesis is mandatory in the Master programme and a prerequisite for admission to the federal examination. To find a supervisor or topic students are directed to the Virtuelle Ausbildungsplattform Medizin (VAM > Masterarbeit), which hosts a "Handbuch", an online Themenbörse to match supervisors and students, a mini‑guide for supervisors and assorted documents. Formal registration steps and deadlines are not specified on this page. Plagiarism rules are explicit: the Faculty policy (22 May 2019) requires supervisors/mentors to check theses (students must consent), and the absence of suspicion must be confirmed at submission; suspected cases are referred to the Masterarbeitskommission. Official guidelines are on VAM and the faculty's plagiarism‑policy PDF; contact: Sandra Lang, Studiendekanat.

process.process_description: Masterstudierende (1. Studienjahr / Beginn 8. Semester) erhalten ab 1. März eine Liste mit angebotenen Masterarbeitsthemen; betreuende Dozierende geben Themen in die Themenbörse ein und können ab 1. März an Studierende des 4. Jahres vergeben. Studierende wählen ein Thema ab 1. März (17:00) und müssen das Learning Agreement bis 31. Juli unterschreiben. Die Arbeit wird in den Semestern 9–11 durchgeführt (Studierende haben insgesamt 16 Wochen Schreibzeit); nicht‑klinische Schwerpunkte in Sem. 9–10, klinische zwischen den Rotationen in Sem. 9–11. Endfassung: spätestens 31. Oktober bei der betreuenden Person; alle Unterlagen inkl. Bewertung bis 30. November im Studiendekanat. Formulare (Learning Agreement, Vorlage, Beurteilungsschema, Eigenständigkeitserklärung u.a.) und Richtlinien sind in der Masterarbeiten-Themenbörse (Menü „Wichtige Dokumente“, Zugang für Dozierende). Betreuer prüfen Plagiate (Turnitin); Einverständnis der Studierenden erforderlich.
